Building a Feature Dataset for Classification

Source: vignettes/feature-dataset.Rmd
feature-dataset.Rmd

The guess_data_type() router is trained on value-profile features (see vignette("feature-engineering")), scored against the example corpora (see vignette("testing-libraries")). This guide shows how those two pieces combine into a single, model-ready feature matrix: one row per column, 477 feature columns, and ontology labels to predict. It is the dataset the vignette("classifier-decision-tree") worked examples are built on.

The modeling unit: a row is a whole column

Each observation is a single column of real tabular data — a vector of values such as c("AUD", "CAD", "CNY", ...). fx_extract_features() turns that vector into 477 numbers describing the shape and content of the whole column: its cardinality, character makeup, numeric range, token vocabulary, and lexicon hits. The classifier learns to recognize a type from how a column looks, exactly the way the router does at inference time.

Two choices keep the task honest:

  • No label leakage. Features are extracted with col_name = NULL, so the column header never enters the feature set.
  • Ground-truth labels. The outcome columns come from a crosswalk, not from running guess_data_type() — so features -> type is a genuine supervised problem, not a model trained to imitate the router.

Three labeled corpora

The builder (data-raw/build_feature_dataset.R) draws one row per column from three sources:

Corpus Rows What it is
Sherlock / VizNet 5,536 Real web-table columns, each tagged with one of 78 semantic types. Labels derive from headers, so this is a value-only signal.
GitTables (dbpedia) 768 Columns from GitHub CSV tables annotated against DBpedia properties; headers anonymized to col0..colN.
formex-native 86 The package’s own curated positive examples, one canonical column per detector; adds clean boolean and structured coverage.
Total 6,390

Sherlock and GitTables labels map to the ontology through the project’s v4 crosswalk CSVs; the formex detector names map through the shipped detector-to-ontology chain. All three resolve data_type, semantic_family, and semantic_type.

A column must clear 8 non-sentinel values to be profiled — a guard that drops columns which are entirely sentinel tokens (all "None", "UNK", "n/a"), since those strip to empty and profile to a degenerate near-empty row.

What a row holds 

d <- readRDS("data-raw/type_features_dataset.rds")
names(d)[1:10]
#> corpus · source_label · vector_length · sample_values ·
#> data_type · semantic_family · semantic_type · format_label ·
#> format_style · unit_type · <477 feature columns>
Column(s) Role
corpus, source_label Provenance: which corpus, and the original label.
vector_length Count of usable (non-missing, non-sentinel) values.
sample_values Up to five example values, joined by ;;.
data_type Coarse target: number, text, categorical, temporal, identifier, structured, boolean.
semantic_family, semantic_type Finer targets (25 / 40 classes).
format_label, format_style, unit_type Deep ontology format axes — mostly empty, since these semantic corpora do not carry them.
477 feature columns The value profile (below).

477 features in 12 blocks

fx_extract_features() computes every block in one pass. A feature that does not apply to a column is NA, never 0.

Block Measures #
core Cardinality, uniqueness, entropy, top-value concentration, Zipf fit. 21
length String-length distribution, fixed-width flag, token counts. 23
charclass Digit / alpha / space / punctuation shares, case patterns. 22
punct Per-symbol presence, counts, and positional spread (22 marks). 118
mask Pattern abstraction (123 Main -> 9 Aaaa), delimiter fields. 21
charfreq Per-letter & per-digit frequencies, first/last-letter distributions. 97
regex ~45 format patterns (email, UUID, dates, money) plus checksums. 43
numeric Numeric summaries, range bounds, Benford, distribution fits. 48
sequence Numeric order: monotonicity, autoincrement, lag-1 autocorrelation. 11
token Token vocabulary, stopword rate, first/last-token stability. 23
lexicon Hit rates against gazetteers (names, cities, states, units). 30
header Column-name keyword flags & input class — all NA here (no headers). 20

Missing data is “not applicable”, so impute by what absence implies

The matrix is deliberately full of NA: numeric statistics are undefined on text, letter frequencies are undefined on all-digit columns. For a model that drops rows with any NA (plain logistic regression), impute each feature by the reason it is missing. data-raw/make_imputation_spec.R writes one rule per feature to type_features_imputation.csv:

Rule # When
zero 412 The structure the feature measures is absent, so FALSE / zero-rate / zero-count is the true value (sequence flags on text, letter/digit/token/lexicon rates, punctuation-position spread, regex checksums with no candidate).
numeric_med + indicator 45 The num_* block, NA because the column is not numeric. Impute the training median and keep coerce_rate_strip as an “is-numeric” indicator, since 0 is a valid number and would forge a measurement.
drop 20 No information: the all-NA nm_* header features and the constant in_is_* flags.

After this, the metadata columns and the three populated label axes have no missing values at all.

Which features fire for a type

For three target types we build a one-vs-rest problem (this type vs. a 500-column sample of everything else) and rank features by univariate discrimination (AUC).

  • us_state — gazetteer hits and shape: lex_us_state_abb_value (0.81), lex_any_value (0.87), pct_all_alpha (0.81), short length. A logistic fit on the top signals reaches ~91% — the one example with real error, since state names overlap city and country.
  • email — has_at and rx_email separate perfectly (AUC 1.0). A lesson in itself: perfect separation breaks unregularized logistic regression, so penalize or read it as a single rule already sufficing.
  • ein — the NN-NNNNNNN pattern (rx_ein, 1.0), a valid IRS prefix (chk_ein_prefix_rate, 1.0), the single dash, and the digit spread.

Where the value signal runs out

Not every type has a surface fingerprint, and the dataset makes that visible:

  • weight is the hardest type. Its one-vs-rest held-out AUC is ~0.50 — no better than a coin flip — because a bare number column is indistinguishable from any other numeric quantity. Its nearest neighbours in feature space are duration, sales, and ranking. The type lives in the header, not the values.
  • city and country are feature twins. They agree on 384 of ~475 features (both short, all-alphabetic, title-cased categoricals) and are split almost entirely by one gazetteer feature, lex_us_city_value (fires on 39% of city values vs 0.3% of country names). That single feature is why the lexicon block exists.

See vignette("classifier-decision-tree") for the modeling that follows from here.

# Reproduce the dataset and its companions:
#   source("data-raw/build_feature_dataset.R")   # the 6,390-row feature matrix
#   source("data-raw/make_imputation_spec.R")    # the per-feature NA rules
#   source("data-raw/model_feature_demo.R")      # the one-vs-rest feature rankings
